newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien, on campaign, says to spend more.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien, on campaign, says to spend more.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, on his first full day of an election campaign, announced on Monday that he would reverse planned spending cuts due to the government's success in cutting its deficit.
"Because we are ahead of schedule on deficit reduction, we can now afford to reinvest in the health care system without jeopardizing our deficit targets," Chretien said in a statement.
"We will act on the recommendation of the National Forum on Health and increase cash transfers to the provinces."
The new measures would take effect in 1998-99.
Specifically, he pledged to raise the cash floor of the Canada Health and Social Transfer (CHST), the block fund transfer to the provinces, to C$12.5 billion from C$11 billion.

His government had cut the CHST cash transfers from C$19.3 billion in 1994-95 to C$14.9 billion in 1996-97, and had scheduled cuts to C$12.5 billion in 1997-98, C$11.8 billion in 1998-99 and less in subsequent years.

"This (announcement) will increase the cash payments and entitlements due the provinces and territories by C$700 million in 1998-99, C$1.4 billion in 1999-00 and 2000-01, C$1.3 billion in 2001-02, and C$1.2 billion in 2002-03," a statement from Chretien's campaign headquarters said.
"In 1996, the Liberal government legislated a guaranteed cash floor of C$11 billion for the CHST," Chretien said.
"Now that we can afford to do more, we will. Our deficit reduction efforts have been far more successful than anyone could have predicted, because of a stronger economy and low interest rates."
"But deficit reduction is not an end in itself. We did it (the reduction) to strengthen the economy and ensure the sustainability of valued social programs like health care," Chretien added.
He pointed out that the February 1997 budget indicated that the 1996-97 deficit, originally set for C$24.3 billion, would be no more than C$19 billion.

"It is not evident that the deficit will be even lower than this most recent estimate," the statement said. "Recent available information indicates the deficit for the first 11 months of 1996-97 is C$7.8 billion."

The statement added: "The final month (March 1997), however, is very important because it includes as much as 30 percent of corporate tax filings. As well, the audited annual financial statement in the fall has in the past included year-end adjustments which have ranged between four and six billion dollars."
All spending commitments in the Liberal platform fall within the framework of existing deficit reduction targets, the statement said.
Both the right-wing Conservative Party and the leftist New Democratic Party said it was trickery to make massive cuts and then to say money was being reinvested.
NDP leader Alexa McDonough said voters would not easily be tricked.

"They're not going to be fooled into thinking that a government that steals your purse like a petty thief and then offers you bus fare to get home at the end of the day is actually addressing your needs," she told a news conference organized by the Canadian Broadcasting Corp.
